AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Glia cells hyperactivity has been proposed to be responsible for chronic pain, however, the mechanisms remain unclear. IL-18, released from glial cells, has been reported to be involved in neuropathic pain. Here, we investigated the role of IL-18 in bone cancer pain.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Bone cancer pain was mimicked by injecting Walker-256 mammary gland carcinoma cells into the intramedullary space of the tibia in rats. Expression and location of IL-18 and IL-18 receptor were tested. To investigate the contribution of IL-18 signaling to bone cancer pain, IL-18-binding protein (IL-18BP) and recombinant IL-18 were used. To investigate the mechanisms of glial cells effects, MK801, NMDA receptor inhibitor and Src kinase-specific inhibitor PP1 also be used.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Tumor cell implantation (TCI) treatment increased expression of IL-18 and IL-18 receptor in spinal cord. The time course of IL-18 upregulation was correlated with TCI-induced pain behaviors. Blocking IL-18 signaling pathway prevented and reversed bone cancer-related pain behaviors. Meanwhile, blocking IL-18 signaling also suppressed TCI-induced glial cells hyperactivity, as well as activation of GluN2B and subsequent Ca(2+)-dependent signaling. Spinal administration of recombinant Il-18 in naïve rat induced significant mechanical allodynia, as well as GluN2B activation. However, intrathecal injection of MK801 failed to suppressed recombinant IL-18-induced GluN2B phosphorylation, while Src kinase inhibitor PP1 significantly inhibited IL-18-induced GluN2B activation.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: IL-18-mediated glial-glia and glia-neuron interaction may facilitate bone cancer pain. Blocking IL-18 signaling may effective prevent and/or suppress bone cancer pain.

AbstractText.Label: PERSPECTIVE ITEM
AbstractText.content: IL-18 signaling may be a new target for cancer pain therapy.
